aiAgentFacts.fact: In 905,543 UK dogs under primary veterinary care in 2016, 1,259 heat-related illness events were identified across 1,222 dogs.
Exertion was the predominant trigger at 74.2% of heat-related illness events; environmental heat accounted for 12.9% and vehicular confinement for 5.2%.
Brachycephalic dogs had greater odds of all three heat-related illness trigger types compared with mesocephalic dogs.
Young male dogs had greater odds of exertional heat-related illness, while older dogs and dogs with respiratory compromise had the greatest odds of the environmental type.
The odds of death following vehicular heat-related illness (OR 1.47) were similar to exertional, and the difference was NOT statistically significant (p = 0.492).
In UK dogs, exertional heat-related illness affects more dogs and kills more dogs than confinement in a hot vehicle — a difference in event frequency, not in per-event lethality.

In a companion VetCompass analysis of severity, the median ambient temperature on days when heat-related illness events occurred was 16.9°C — heat-related illness is not confined to heatwave conditions.
The study counts only events that reached a veterinary practice; dogs that recovered at home or died before arrival are not represented.

historyQuestions: Not prescribed by this paper. Its risk stratification does support establishing trigger context — exertional versus environmental versus confinement — alongside skull shape, age and any respiratory compromise.
redFlags: Not defined by this study. Heat-related illness is a recognised emergency, but this paper reports epidemiology and does not enumerate clinical red flags or grading criteria.
differentialDiagnosesMentioned: Not addressed — the study classifies confirmed heat-related illness events by trigger and does not evaluate differential diagnosis.
recommendedDiagnosticWorkups: Not addressed — no diagnostic workup is evaluated or recommended by this study.
urgentCareTriggers: Suspected overheating requires immediate veterinary contact. This is a standing safety boundary, not a finding of this study — the paper evaluates no triage threshold, and first-aid or cooling guidance must come from a veterinarian rather than from this record.

limitations: Ascertainment: only events presenting to a veterinary practice were captured — home-recovered and pre-arrival deaths are absent, so trigger proportions describe presenting cases
Single country (UK) and single year (2016); climate, culture and exercise habits limit transfer to other populations
The vehicular-versus-exertional death odds comparison (OR 1.47) was not statistically significant (p = 0.492) and must not be reported as a difference
No safe temperature, duration, or activity threshold is defined for any individual dog
No prevention or treatment strategy was evaluated; any 'walk earlier' style advice is inference from the trigger distribution, not a tested intervention
Retrospective clinical records were not primarily recorded for research, so trigger classification depends on what practitioners documented at the time
